short_bio: Founder of the medieval Chola line. He captured Thanjavur from the Muttarayars and established it as the capital, laying the foundation for the later imperial expansion.
Son of Vijayalaya. He expanded the kingdom by defeating the Pallavas and consolidating Chola power in the Kaveri region.
Long-reigning ruler known as Maduraikonda. He captured Madurai and extended Chola authority, though the later part of his reign saw pressure from the Rashtrakutas.
Son of Parantaka I. His reign appears to have been relatively short. He is remembered as a devotee and patron; his son Uttama later succeeded to the throne.
Younger brother of Gandaraditya and third son of Parantaka I. He ruled only briefly before being succeeded by his son Parantaka II (Sundara Chola).
Also known as Sundara Chola. Son of Arinjaya. He recovered some lost territory and is the father of Rajaraja I. His reign saw the rise of his son Aditya II as co-regent.

Also known as Aditha Karikalan, he was a co-regent of the Chola Empire in South India. As the eldest son of Emperor Parantaka Chola II (Sundara Chola), he was the designated heir apparent to the throne and the older brother of the famous Rajaraja Chola I and Princess Kundavai. His life, military prowess, and untimely death remain one of the most compelling chapters in South Indian history.

Also known as Madhurantaka, he was the son of King Gandaraditya and the famously pious queen Sembiyan Mahadevi. His reign was a critical period of peace, domestic consolidation, and administrative growth that laid the structural foundation for the massive maritime expansions of his successor, Rajaraja Chola I.

common_titles: Rajakesarivarman, mummudi chola, pandyakulasani, keralantaka, simhalantaka, sivapadasekharan
short_bio: One of the greatest Chola emperors. Born Arulmozhi Varman, he expanded the empire into Sri Lanka, the Chera country, and the Maldives, and built the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur.

Son of Rajaraja I. He completed the conquest of Sri Lanka, led the famous Ganges expedition, and founded the new capital Gangaikondacholapuram. His reign marks the greatest extent of the Chola empire.
Son of Rajendra I. A warrior king who continued campaigns against the Western Chalukyas and was killed at the battle of Koppam.
Succeeded his brother Rajadhiraja I. He continued the struggle with the Western Chalukyas and maintained the empire’s strength.
Brother of Rajendra II. He fought successfully against the Western Chalukyas and maintained Chola power until his death.
Son of Virarajendra. His short reign ended amid civil disturbance; he was succeeded by Kulottunga I, beginning the Later Chola line.

common_titles: Rajakesarivarman, Chakravartigal, Rajanarayana, Tribhuvana Chakravartigal, Konerinmaikondaan, Sungam Thavirtha Cholan, Jayadhara, Virudarajabhayankara
short_bio: Founder of the Later Chola (Chalukya-Chola) line. Son of the Eastern Chalukya Rajaraja Narendra and a Chola princess. His long reign was marked by administrative stability and consolidation of Vengi.
Son of Kulottunga I. He recovered Vengi and Gangavadi and continued the stable Later Chola administration.
Son of Vikrama Chola. His reign was relatively peaceful and continued the Later Chola line.
Later Chola ruler known for the construction of the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. He maintained the empire during a period of gradual transition.
Later Chola king who ruled during the rising power of the Pandyas. His reign saw increasing external pressures.
Long-reigning Later Chola. He intervened in Pandya succession disputes but faced the growing strength of Maravarman Sundara Pandya I.
Later Chola ruler who reigned under increasing Pandya dominance. The Chola kingdom had become largely subordinate by this period.
Last independent Chola emperor. He was defeated by Maravarman Kulasekara Pandya I around 1279, marking the end of the Chola empire.

Some of the Chola Kings whose identification is missing/unclear. Many Kings held the title "Parakesarivarman" and "Rajakesarivarman", which makes it difficult to identify the King. Other Kings share the same name and title, in which case the possible identifications have been listed below.
Traditional founder of the First Pandya Empire after the Kalabhra interregnum. He is credited with restoring Pandya power in the Tamil country.
Early ruler of the First Pandya Empire. Succeeded Kadungon and continued the restoration of Pandya authority.
Also known as Jayantavarman or Seliyan Sendan. An early First Empire ruler whose reign is known mainly from later traditional accounts and limited inscriptions.
Important early Pandya ruler. He is associated with victories that strengthened the First Empire and is mentioned in later records and literary traditions.
Son or successor of Arikesari. He continued the expansion and consolidation of the First Pandya Empire.
Also called Pallavabhanjana. A significant First Empire ruler known for military activity against the Pallavas and for temple patronage.
Also known as Varaguna Maharaja and Nedunjadayan. One of the better-documented First Empire rulers, known for extensive temple grants and military campaigns.
Powerful First Empire ruler. He faced invasions from the Rashtrakutas and Sri Lanka but maintained Pandya power for much of his long reign.
Successor of Srimara Srivallabha. His reign saw continued challenges from external powers.
Later First Empire ruler. His reign forms part of the transition toward the period of Chola dominance.
Last significant ruler of the First Empire before the major Chola conquest under Parantaka I. He is said to have fled to Sri Lanka after defeat.
Mentioned in some traditional sequences. Insufficient contemporary evidence for a secure chronology.
Medieval Pandya ruler known from limited inscriptions, mainly in the Tirunelveli region. He appears to have maintained local authority during the period of Chola overlordship.
One of the claimants in the mid-12th-century Pandya civil war. He is associated with Chola support against his rival Parakrama.
Rival claimant in the 12th-century Pandya succession conflict. He received support from Sri Lanka against Kulasekhara.
Son of the civil-war claimant Kulasekhara. Limited independent evidence for his rule.
Son of the civil-war claimant Parakrama. Mentioned in the context of the succession struggle.

Jatavarman Kulasekhara I served as a Pandyan monarch who ruled during a period of rising regional power and military campaigns. His reign helped consolidate Pandyan authority in southern India prior to the major imperial expansions led by his successors.
meykirti_original:
He ruled before the period of Pandyan revival. He succeeded his father Vikrama Pandya of the civil war.
During his reign, he withheld tribute from the Chola empire while Kulothunga Chola III fought the Hoysalas. This rebellion provoked a Chola invasion in 1205. The invaders sacked Madurai and destroyed the ancient coronation hall. Kulasekhara fled before surrendering with his family. Kulothunga restored the crown under Chola suzerainty. This defeat set the stage for later Pandyan retaliation under his successor Maravarman Sundara Pandya I.

short_bio: Founder of the second Pandya empire. He invaded the Chola country, sacked Thanjavur and Uraiyur, and forced the submission of Kulottunga III, beginning the period of Pandya ascendancy.
meykirti_original:
He reversed centuries of Chola dominance and founded the second Pandyan empire, establishing the Pandyas as the paramount power in South India. 
To avenge the prior destruction of Madurai, he invaded the Chola heartland, sacked Thanjavur and Uraiyur, and drove the Chola monarchs into exile. He performed a virabhisheka at the Chola coronation hall in Ayirattali and conducted a thulabaram at the Chidambaram temple. After Hoysala intervention threatened his forces, he restored the Chola crown only after extracting formal submission at Pon Amaravathi. He subsequently repelled Oriya incursions at Srirangam and allied with the Kadava chieftain Kopperunchinga I against Chola and Hoysala influence, laying the foundation for enduring Pandyan ascendancy.

short_bio: Brief successor of Maravarman Sundara I. His short reign forms part of the transition to the more powerful rulers of the mid-13th century.
Ruled during the early phase of the second empire. He maintained Pandya power before the major expansions under Jatavarman Sundara I.

common_titles: ponveindha perumal, hemachadana raja, emmandalamum kondaruliya, tribhuvanachakravarti
short_bio: One of the most powerful Pandya emperors. He expanded the kingdom into the Chola country, southern Andhra, Kerala, and northern Sri Lanka.
Co-ruler or sub-king during the reigns of Jatavarman Sundara I and early Maravarman Kulasekara I. Shared rule was common in this period.
Last great independent Pandya emperor. He defeated Rajendra III and the Hoysalas (c. 1279), ending Chola power. His death led to a destructive civil war between his sons.
Co-ruler during the long reign of Maravarman Kulasekara I. One of several princes who shared authority in the late 13th century.
Co-ruler contemporary with Maravarman Kulasekara I and Jatavarman Sundara II. Part of the system of shared rule.
One of the sons or claimants after Maravarman Kulasekara I. Involved in the civil war that followed the emperor’s death.
Another major claimant in the civil war after Maravarman Kulasekara I. Multiple Sundara Pandyas are known from this turbulent period.
Later Pandya ruler known from limited records. The period after the civil war and Muslim invasions is poorly documented.
Mentioned among the later Pandya rulers. Limited secure evidence for a precise reign.
